food.text: By the 19th century, corn had become the second most important cereal in Egypt. Maize had been imported from Mesoamerica in the 17th century and introduced new varieties of bread to Egyptian tables.

The earliest written references to falafel from Egyptian sources date to the 19th century, even though it has been speculated that the dish goes back to Pharaonic Egypt. Oil was probably too expensive to use for deep frying in ancient Egypt, and the dish most likely originated in Egypt.

In the mid-19th century, French-trained chefs worked in khedival palace kitchens and luxury hotels in Egypt. They introduced European culinary techniques that Egyptian cooks later adopted. The pasta bake macarona bil-bechamel, with its meat sauce and béchamel, traces its origins to these chefs.

In 1853, explorer Richard Burton documented koshary in his book Journey to Egypt and the Hijaz as the breakfast meal of the people of Suez. It consisted of Egyptian lentils, rice, butter, onions and pickled lemons. This account is thought to be the earliest known English-language written reference to koshary.
tags: Journey to Egypt and the Hijaz

art.text: Neo-Mamluk architecture was popular mainly in Egypt in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It combined the principles of modern European architecture with stylistic elements of historic Mamluk architecture. It was used for government buildings, mosques and residential buildings.
Egyptian modern art was institutionalized by the creation of the Prince Youssef Kamel Art School in 1908. That step later helped the scene shift toward what became Egyptian contemporary art.
Until 1835, the pink granite obelisk at Luxor Temple was one of a matching pair. In that year the other obelisk was taken to Paris, where it now stands in the centre of the Place de la Concorde.

Muhammad Ali hired the French architect Pascal Coste as chief engineer from 1818 to 1827 and asked him to design a new mosque in the Citadel of Cairo. Coste proposed a Neo-Mamluk design as a "national style" for Egypt, but Muhammad Ali rejected it. Another architect finished the mosque in an Ottoman style with European influences.

The al-Rifa'i Mosque in Cairo was commissioned in 1869 and begun by the Egyptian architect Husayn Fahmi Pasha. Construction stopped in 1880 and restarted in 1906 under Max Herz, and the mosque was finally completed in 1912.

Saint Mark's Coptic Orthodox Cathedral in Azbakeya, Cairo, built in the late eighteenth century, marked the start of a Coptic architectural revival; it became the seat of the Coptic Pope in 1800. Ottoman rules against building new churches were progressively eased afterwards, allowing many churches to be rebuilt after more than three hundred years of restrictions.
Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida was set in ancient Egypt. It was commissioned by the Khedive of Ottoman Egypt for its premiere in Cairo in 1871.
art.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

art.text: When Max Herz took over the al-Rifa'i Mosque in 1906, he felt Husayn Fahmi Pasha's emphasis on symmetry strayed from a purer Mamluk style. It was too late for major changes to the plan. Herz instead made the references to certain Mamluk-era details more explicit.

The Egyptian Ministry of Awqaf promoted Neo-Mamluk building, and its projects were especially numerous from 1884 to 1913. A report by Saber Sabri, its chief engineer from 1892 to 1906, indicates that most new buildings during his tenure were in the Neo-Mamluk style.
The Cairo Railway Station opened in 1856 but was destroyed by fire in 1882. It was rebuilt between 1891 and 1893 in a Neo-Mamluk style, with Husayn Fahmi Pasha as the architect.

David Roberts began his journey in August 1838, landing at Alexandria and spending the rest of the year in Cairo. He returned to Britain at the end of 1839 after falling ill, having spent 11 months in the region. In 1840 the publisher F.G. Moon paid him £3,000 for the copyright to his 272 watercolour sketches.
art.source_title: The Holy Land, Syria, Idumea, Arabia, Egypt, and Nubia
tags: The Holy Land, Egypt and Nubia

art.text: In 1889 the French archaeologist Albert Gayet published a catalogue of Coptic art. At the Bulaq Museum he staged the first exhibition of Coptic monuments. Tens of thousands of coloured fragments then found their way into the museums of the world.
The Egyptian National Library (Dar al-Kutub) was built in 1904 and designed by Alfonso Manescalo. It is attached to the Museum of Islamic Art and is listed among the Neo-Mamluk buildings.

war.text: In 1882 the United Kingdom fought mostly Egyptian and Sudanese forces under Ahmed 'Urabi, an army officer who had mutinied against Khedive Tewfik Pasha in 1881. At Tell El Kebir the British lost 900 troops and killed approximately two thousand Egyptians, and some British soldiers captured by the Egyptians were brutally tortured to death. The war ended in British occupation of Egypt and the trial and exile of 'Urabi. The Ottoman Empire's already weak authority over Egypt became nominal.

On the morning of 16 November 1875, an Egyptian force marching through a narrow mountain pass at Gundet was ambushed by Ethiopian warriors who sallied forth from hiding places up the slope and charged down on the shocked Egyptian columns. The Egyptians were vastly outnumbered and taken completely by surprise, which nullified their advantage in firepower and caused many of the unenthusiastic fellahin soldiers to rout. The expeditionary force was annihilated: about 2,000 Egyptians perished, including its commander, Colonel Adolph Arendrup, and its guns and rocket-stands fell into Ethiopian hands.

Muhammad Ali ruled Egypt from 1805 to 1848 and by 1840 controlled Egypt, Sudan, Hejaz, the Levant, Cyprus, Crete and parts of Greece. He had risen by a violent purge of the Mamluks: on 1 March 1811 he invited their leaders to a celebration at the Cairo Citadel, surrounded them there and had them killed, then sent his army through Egypt to rout the rest. He recaptured the Arabian territories for the sultan, where Abdullah ibn Saud was sent to Constantinople and executed, and conquered Sudan on his own, a reign remembered in Sudan as brutal and heavy-handed. His attempt to suppress the Greek rebellion failed after European powers intervened at Navarino, where the entire Egyptian navy was sunk.

On 31 October 1831, an Egyptian army under Ibrahim Pasha invaded Syria, starting the First Turko-Egyptian War. The stated pretext was a quarrel with Abdullah Pasha of Acre. Muhammad Ali alleged that 6,000 fellahin had fled to Acre to escape the draft, corvée and taxes, and he wanted them back. The only significant resistance was at Acre, which fell after a six-month siege from 3 November 1831 to 27 May 1832, while Ali squeezed Egypt harder to pay for the campaign and his people resented the burden.

In 1813 Muhammad Ali Pasha went in person to Arabia to signal reestablished authority. He arrived at Jeddah in September with 2,000 infantry, 2,000 cavalry and 8,000 camels. The camels carried a large amount of supplies and ammunition for the Ottoman army.

In 1839 the Ottoman fleet sailed to Alexandria and surrendered to Muhammad Ali, after Ottoman defeat at Nezib. Britain and Austria then intervened, and on 27 November 1840 the Convention of Alexandria was agreed. Egypt abandoned its claims to Syria and returned the Ottoman fleet, and Muhammad Ali and his sons were recognized as Egypt's legitimate rulers.

In 1801 a British expeditionary force, working with Ottoman forces, set out to free Egypt from French occupation. After victories at Abukir, Mandora and Alexandria, the British captured Cairo and besieged Alexandria from 17 August. Menou capitulated on 2 September and signed over to Britain the Egyptian antiquities the French had collected, including the Rosetta Stone.
war.source_title: French invasion of Egypt and Syria

war.text: In the 1890s Britain wanted to control the Nile partly to safeguard a planned irrigation dam at Aswan. Herbert Kitchener led military campaigns against Mahdist Sudan from 1896 to 1898. They culminated in the Battle of Omdurman on 2 September 1898.

On 20 May 1882, British and French warships arrived off the coast of Alexandria. On 11 June an anti-European riot in the city killed 50 Europeans. Colonel 'Urabi ordered his forces to put down the riot, but Europeans fled the city and his army began fortifying the town while the French fleet was recalled to France. From 11 to 13 July the British fleet bombarded Alexandria, and much of the city was destroyed by fires caused by explosive shells and, according to contemporary British sources, by 'Urabists seeking to ruin the city that the British were taking over.

The Egyptian Khedive first heard about American military methods from Thaddeus P. Mott, an ex-Union artillery officer he met in Constantinople in 1868. Mott convinced him to hire American veterans to modernize Egypt's armed forces. In 1870 the first of them arrived: ex-Confederate officers Henry Hopkins Sibley and William Wing Loring.

Ibrahim's forces reached the Wahhabi capital Diriyah by April 1818 and besieged it until September, waiting for Saudi supplies to run out. On 11 September, Abdullah Ibn Saud sued for peace and offered his surrender in exchange for sparing Diriyah, but Ibrahim Pasha ordered the city razed to the ground anyway. Abdullah was taken captive and sent to Istanbul, where he was beheaded in December alongside several other Wahhabi Imams on the orders of Sultan Mahmud II, and his corpse was publicly displayed.

On 11 September 1840, Commodore Charles Napier bombarded Beirut and landed at Jounieh with 1,500 Turks and Marines. Until then his small force could do little against 15,000 Egyptian troops. The Syrian population had revolted against Muhammad Ali's army, so Ibrahim could do no more than try to hold the coastal cities.

In 1821 the Turco-Egyptian conquest ended the Funj Sultanate of Sudan. Muhammad Adlan, who prepared to resist by ordering the army mustered at the Nile confluence, was assassinated in a plot near Sennar in early 1821. One of the murderers, a man named Daf'Allah, then rode back to the capital to prepare Sultan Badi VII's submission ceremony to the Turks. On 14 June the invaders received Badi VII's official submission at Sennar, a city once famed for wealth and splendour that they found reduced to a heap of ruins.

William Wing Loring became Inspector-General of the Egyptian army and in 1875 chief of staff of the expedition in Ethiopia. He took part in the Battle of Gura, which ended in defeat. Egyptians blamed the Americans for the disaster, and Loring, Sibley and the other officers endured two years of frustration and humiliation in Cairo.

literature.text: Percy Bysshe Shelley's "Ozymandias" (1818) is one of the most enduring literary treatments of ancient Egypt to come out of the 19th-century Romantic movement. It shows how Egypt served Western writers as a symbol of timeless grandeur.
literature.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

literature.text: Egyptian hieroglyphs were totally inscrutable from roughly the 5th century CE until their decipherment in the early 19th century. Scribes had long since stopped studying to read them, which left Egypt's own recorded history inaccessible.
literature.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

literature.text: In 1914 Muhammad Husayn Haykal wrote Zaynab, which is considered the first modern Egyptian novel as well as the first Islamic novel. It marked a turning point for Egyptian fiction just as the Industrial era closed.

The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, gave scholars the resources to decipher Egyptian texts. The key breakthroughs came more than twenty years later, when Jean-François Champollion worked out hieroglyphs and Thomas Young worked out Demotic. By Champollion's death in 1832, the general sense of Egyptian texts could be discerned.

The Holy Land, Syria, Idumea, Arabia, Egypt, and Nubia was a travelogue containing 250 lithographs by Louis Haghe after David Roberts's watercolor sketches. It was published by subscription between 1842 and 1849. It was one of the most expensive publications of the nineteenth century.
literature.source_title: The Holy Land, Syria, Idumea, Arabia, Egypt, and Nubia
tags: The Holy Land, Egypt and Nubia

literature.text: The Rosetta Stone was discovered on July 15, 1799, in the port town of Rosetta, Egypt, and has been held in the British Museum since 1802. Because it carries Greek, Demotic and hieroglyphic text, linguists could use Greek to decipher hieroglyphs and translate hundreds of texts.

Emmanuel de Rougé was the first scholar able to read an Egyptian text in full. In 1856 he published the first translations of Egyptian literary texts, opening ancient Egyptian writing to modern readers.

In 1884 Muhammad Abduh and Jamāl al-Dīn al-Afghānī founded the journal Al-Urwah al-Wuthqa, a pan-Islamic revolutionary literary and political publication. It ran only from March to October and was banned by British authorities in Egypt and India. Even so, it circulated from Morocco to India and is considered one of the first and most important publications of the Nahda.

The almah (plural awalim) were educated Egyptian women, a class of courtesans or female entertainers, trained to sing and recite classical Arabic poetry and to discourse wittily. According to Edward William Lane, they were first introduced as singers, not dancers or prostitutes, and at weddings and other respectable festivities they sang from behind a screen or from another room without displaying themselves. In the 19th century the word came to be used for all the erotic local dancers, who usually came from very poor backgrounds and sometimes took part in sexual acts in return for money, and in 1834 all their performances were banned as 'unclassy'.
Muhammad Abduh, a major figure of Islamic modernism, authored the influential Risālat at-Tawḥīd in 1897. In 1911 he published Sharḥ Nahj al-Balagha.

The text accompanying David Roberts's images was mostly written by two authors. George Croly wrote the historical portions, while William Brockedon wrote the descriptive ones. Their words accompanied the lithographs of Louis Haghe.
literature.source_title: The Holy Land, Syria, Idumea, Arabia, Egypt, and Nubia
tags: The Holy Land, Egypt and Nubia

literature.text: Professor Annabel Wharton said the Roberts work has "proved to be the most pervasive and enduring of the nineteenth-century renderings of the East circulated in the West." The Metropolitan Museum of Art described its lithographer Louis Haghe as "the best and most prolific lithographer of the time".
literature.source_title: The Holy Land, Syria, Idumea, Arabia, Egypt, and Nubia
tags: The Holy Land, Egypt and Nubia

science.text: For roughly 1,300 years, from about the 5th century CE, nobody could read Egyptian hieroglyphs, because scribes no longer studied them. In 1824, Jean-François Champollion decrypted the script. That ended the long period in which Egypt's own recorded history had been inaccessible.
science.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

science.text: Under Muhammad Ali, whose reign ran from 1805 to 1848, Egypt revived learning through educational reform and cultural investment. The Institut d'Égypte was reconstituted in 1836 as The Egyptian Society, focused on antiquities and book collection. By 1880 its mission included medicine, agriculture, Egyptology, and the sciences.

Deciphering hieroglyphs allowed the translation of hundreds of texts and inscriptions that had been indecipherable. This gave insight into Egyptian culture that might otherwise have been lost. The Rosetta Stone, which carried the same text in Greek, Demotic and hieroglyphs, has been held in the British Museum since 1802.

Before Champollion's decipherment, inscriptions had been thought to hold occult wisdom. The decryption showed they were nothing more than royal names and titles, funerary formulae, and boastful accounts of military campaigns. The new knowledge was widely read as exposing a mythical Egypt as an illusion created by Greek and Western imaginations.
science.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

science.text: In 1859, a new branch of the Egyptian Society, the reconstituted Institut d'Égypte, opened in Alexandria under the same name. It was supported by Egyptian and European scholars. In 1880 the headquarters moved back to Cairo.
Scientific and intellectual life diversified under Khedive Ismail and his successors. In 1875 the Geographic Society was founded with a mission to carry out geographic research, especially in Africa.

The Agricultural Society was founded in Egypt in 1898 to improve cultivation and combat pests. It was one of several scientific and cultural associations that emerged in the decades after the Institut d'Égypte was revived.

politics.text: Muhammad Ali, an Albanian commander sent to drive out Napoleon's forces, was named Wali (governor) of Egypt in 1805. He rose to power through political maneuvers and went on to be widely considered the founder of modern Egypt.

The Ottoman sultan granted Muhammad Ali's grandson Isma'il Pasha the title of Khedive in 1867, along with near-total autonomy over internal affairs. The Khedivate of Egypt remained a tributary state of the Ottoman Empire, ruled by members of Muhammad Ali's dynasty.

In 1882 British forces occupied Egypt during the Anglo-Egyptian War. The occupation lasted exactly 40 years, until Egypt's independence was declared in 1922. The first period, from 1882 to 1914, is often called the "veiled protectorate".
politics.source_title: History of Egypt under the British

politics.text: At the height of his power in 1840, Muhammad Ali of Egypt ruled Egypt, Sudan, the Levant, Hejaz, Cyprus and Crete. This vast empire made Cairo far more than an ordinary Ottoman provincial capital.

In the 1800s the Funj and Darfur Sultanates collapsed in the wake of Turco-Egyptian invasions. The Funj Sultanate, established in 1504, had been the first Muslim polity in the region and had attracted Sufi scholars and religious teachers from Egypt and the Hejaz.

The Mahdist movement began in 1881 when Muhammad Ahmad proclaimed himself the 'Mahdi', the 'expected one' of Islam. He declared a jihad against the Egyptian- and Turkish-dominated administration in Khartoum, and his followers became known as the Ansar. After they overthrew that administration, they set up an 'Islamic and national' government that forced the Coptic Christians, a substantial part of the population, to convert to Islam, and later severely persecuted Christians. Famine, war, disease and persecution cut Sudan's population by about half, from roughly 8 million to barely 2.5 million.

Muhammad Ali initiated a violent purge of the Mamluks, consolidating his rule and permanently ending their hold over Egypt. The massacre of the Mamluks took place in 1811, and it eliminated a faction that had competed for power in the country.

Muhammad Ali's power reached its height in 1840, when he controlled Egypt, Sudan, Hejaz, the Levant, Cyprus, Crete and parts of Greece. He transformed Cairo from a mere Ottoman provincial capital into the center of an expansive empire.

Muhammad Ali went to war against the sultan in 1831. His army overran Syria, took Acre after a six-month siege, then marched into Anatolia and soundly defeated the Ottoman army at Konya, leaving no military obstacle between it and Constantinople. The European powers forced him to retreat. In 1840 a British and Austrian naval blockade and an attack on Acre brought him to accept terms, and in 1842 he took a brokered peace in which he and his descendants were granted hereditary rule over Egypt and Sudan.

The Khedives' reform projects were costly and incurred serious foreign debts, which allowed European powers to increase their influence over Egyptian affairs. Nationalist sentiment grew in opposition and led to the Urabi revolution between 1879 and 1882. The revolution was crushed by force: in 1882 British naval forces shelled and captured Alexandria, then the British army landed and defeated Urabi's army at the Battle of Tel el-Kebir. Urabi was tried for treason and sentenced to death, but the sentence was commuted to exile.

In 1879 the Ottoman sultan colluded with the Great Powers to depose Isma'il in favor of his son Tewfik. Three years later the United Kingdom invaded, ostensibly to support Tewfik against Ahmed Orabi's nationalist government. After that, ultimate power resided with the British High Commissioner.

Muhammad Ali and his successors used the title Khedive long before it was official, but the Sublime Porte did not sanction it until 1867. Isma'il secured recognition of Egypt's virtual independence through a mixture of flattery and bribery, unlike his grandfather's policy of war against the Porte.

In 1914 the Ottoman Empire joined World War I on the side of the Central Powers, and Britain declared a protectorate over Egypt. Khedive Abbas II was deposed, and his successor Hussein Kamel was compelled to declare himself Sultan of Egypt independent of the Ottomans in December 1914.
politics.source_title: History of Egypt under the British

politics.text: The Egyptian Fundamental Ordinance of 1882 followed an abortive attempt to promulgate a constitution in 1879. It was limited in scope and was effectively more an organic law of the Consultative Council to the khedive than a true constitution.
politics.source_title: History of Egypt under the British

politics.text: In 1847 Muhammad Ali laid the foundation stone of a great bridge across the Nile at the start of the Delta. By June 1848 his mind had given way and he could no longer govern. In September 1848 the Porte acknowledged Ibrahim as ruler of the pashalik, but Ibrahim died in November.

philosophy.text: In 1824 Jean-François Champollion deciphered Egyptian hieroglyphs, a script that had been inscrutable since roughly the 5th century CE. Inscriptions that a century earlier had been thought to hold occult wisdom proved to be royal names and titles, funerary formulae and boastful accounts of military campaigns.
philosophy.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

philosophy.text: Rifa'a at-Tahtawi went to Paris in 1826 as chaplain to a group of Egyptian students, intended to be an imam. According to his memoir, he studied ethics, social and political philosophy, and mathematics, and read Condillac, Voltaire, Rousseau and Montesquieu.

Muhammad Abduh began teaching esoteric Islamic texts to advanced students at Al-Azhar while still a student there. From 1877 he taught logic, theology, ethics and politics. He later wrote Risalat at-Tawhid, 'The Theology of Unity', and a commentary on the Quran.

Islamic modernism tried to reconcile the Islamic faith with modern values such as democracy, civil rights, rationality and equality. It has been called the first Muslim ideological response to the Western cultural challenge. It insisted on religious faith in public life, unlike secularism.

Qasim Amin, called one of the Arab world's first feminists, criticised veiling, seclusion, early marriage and the lack of education for Muslim women. He argued the Quran does not teach women's subjugation but supports their rights, and he backed his beliefs with Quranic verses.

The Nahda, or 'the Awakening', was a cultural movement in Arab regions of the Ottoman Empire, including Egypt. It flourished in the second half of the 19th century. Traditional scholarship linked it to Napoleon's 1798 invasion, but recent scholarship sees it as partly 'autogenetic', not only Western-inspired.

The explosion of new knowledge about actual Egyptian religion, wisdom and philosophy was widely interpreted as exposing the mythical image of Egypt as an illusion created by Greek and Western imaginations. Still, the article notes that an obscure part of the inscriptions might agree with the mystic vision.
philosophy.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

philosophy.text: Three of Rifa'a at-Tahtawi's published volumes were works of political and moral philosophy. They introduced Egyptian readers to Enlightenment ideas such as secular authority, political rights and liberty. He also wrote about what made a 'good Egyptian' and about the public good.

Islamic modernist thinkers regarded Islam as compatible with Western philosophy and modern science. Major figures included Hassan al-Attar, the Grand Imam of al-Azhar who died in 1835, and Jamal al-Din Afghani. Egyptian Nahda figure Rifa'a al-Tahtawi helped bring Western ethical notions into Muslim communities.

Qasim Amin was greatly influenced by Darwin and argued for modernising Egypt along European lines. He was also influenced by Herbert Spencer and John Stuart Mill, who argued for equality of the sexes. He believed raising women's status would greatly improve the nation.

Muhammad Abduh stated that every society should be allowed to choose a suitable form of government based on its history and present circumstances. He was exiled from Egypt in 1882 for six years for supporting the Urabi revolt. In Beirut he worked to further respect and friendship between Islam, Christianity and Judaism.

Rifa'a at-Tahtawi's work was the first effort in what became the Egyptian renaissance, the nahda, which flourished between 1860 and 1940. His School of Languages, founded in 1835, graduated the earliest modern Egyptian intellectual milieu.

Muhammad Abduh joined Freemasonry alongside his mentor al-Afghani and other pupils, subscribing to various Masonic lodges. He eventually left the secret society in his later years. He and al-Afghani also published the journal al-'Urwa al-Wuthqa in Paris in 1884.

culture.text: In the 19th century, European visitors left graffiti on the walls of the Temple of Dendur while it still stood beside the Nile in Nubia. British naval officer Armar Lowry Corry carved a prominent inscription reading "A L Corry RN 1817" on the left side as one enters the temple.

Many Egyptian Copts immigrated to Sudan in the early nineteenth century, and they initially received tolerant treatment. Under the Mahdist State (1881-98), they were persecuted, and many were forced to renounce their faith in favour of Islam and to intermarry with Sudanese people. Copts have historically faced persecution in Sudan, with their numbers now put at 400,000 to 500,000.

At the end of the 18th century, Ottoman Egypt had a small Greek community of under a thousand to 5000 people. It was split into two communities that rarely intermingled, one of them mostly merchants who were Arabic-speaking descendants of early settlers or who arrived after 1517.

European visitors left graffiti on the walls of the Temple of Dendur in Nubia in the 19th century. British naval officer Armar Lowry Corry carved the prominent inscription "A L Corry RN 1817" on the left as one enters. Italian Egyptologist Girolamo Segato also left an inscription.

Italian Egyptologist Girolamo Segato also left a graffiti inscription on the Temple of Dendur. Visitors had been carving their marks there since as early as 10 BCE, when one carved an oath near the image of Pihor.

France occupied Egypt during the War of the Second Coalition and established cordial relations with the Greek community. On 27 June 1800, a Greek unit called the Légion Grecque was formed under Nikolaos Papazoglou, numbering 577 officers and soldiers.

Greek communities spread across Egypt in the 19th century. Zagazig's was founded in 1850, Mansoura's in 1860, Port Said's in 1870 and Tanta's in 1880, while Minia in Upper Egypt, founded in 1812, was the region's oldest.

After the Mahdist State (1881-98) had persecuted them, forcing many to renounce their faith in favour of Islam and to intermarry with Sudanese people, the Anglo-Egyptian invasion gave Sudan's Copts greater religious and economic liberties. This enabled them to enter sectors like banking, engineering, medicine and the civil service.

Cairo's first organised Greek community was founded in 1856, with its patriarchate based at Saint Nicholas Greek Orthodox Cathedral in Hamzaoui. The monastery of Saint George in Old Cairo, which held a Greek hospital, a school and housing for the elderly and poor, still survives.

Sultan Abdul Hamid II resettled many Greek Muslims from Crete in Egypt, Libya, Lebanon and Syria after the Greco-Turkish War of 1897. This war resulted in the autonomy of Crete, and the newcomers are often confusingly called Cretan Turks.
